Disasters and Emergency Response.text: Japan lives with earthquakes, typhoons, floods, landslides and fires, and its emergency system is older than the hero system and still runs every disaster. Phones blare national alerts, sirens and loudspeakers order evacuations, schools and offices drill every year, and every neighborhood has a marked evacuation site, usually a school ground or a park. Fire departments, police and city crews run the response; rescue heroes are called in by agency or by name, and the first pro on scene reports to the incident commander. Rescue specialists are among the most respected pros: Thirteen, the Wild Wild Pussycats and every hero whose Quirk can dig, fly, lift, cool or sense. The order never changes: get people out, treat the injured, stop the spread, then clear and rebuild. Unlicensed people may carry, guide and give first aid, but a Quirk used in a rescue without a license still brings a police statement afterward. Typhoons come in late summer and autumn with a day or two of warning; earthquakes come with none. Afterward shelters fill, trains stop, convenience stores empty, volunteers arrive, and the news replays footage of the heroes who were there.
